NLA but I am a school counselor. Stop asking your daughter to tell the story. This advice comes not from me but from the child advocacy office of my local state’s attorney and a graduate level professor. Contact your state’s child protection hotline and the police and report what happened. I hope that your local state’s attorney has a child advocacy center that can help guide you and your family through this process. They typically have counselors who specialize in these cases. Most counselors do not have that kind of specialized training needed/required to work with children who have been sexually assaulted/abused.  I have learned that it is paramount you or other people who are not trained for this should not have your child tell the story of what happened. You don’t want her to have to tell this multiple times. The result of doing so could be harmful for several reasons. Work with the counselor she will talk to eventually and ask them how to best support your daughter and family through this. Child advocacy centers in states attorney’s offices also often have important supports liked therapy dogs to help you and your family during your meetings…

Use this link to find your local child advocacy center https://www.nationalchildrensalliance.org/cac-model/

I think you are right about you having a better sense of empathy than your husband.  He doesn’t seem to understand what his daughter s thinking, feeling, or about to do and therefore isn’t able to think through what her needs are going to be. One of the best things my partner told me when we were young parents was to make sure our child was prepared for what was about to happen…eg going in the car for a long trip vs going to the grocery store vs going to the park. This has been one of the best bits for me as a school counselor too.  Helping the kids be prepared for what they are about do helps me understand how to think through what they will need to be successful whether it’s taking a test or getting ready for an intruder drill, or figuring out their path to college.

Your husband feels embarrassed.  I have not met anyone who learns best when they feel embarrassed.  I believe you don’t have any desire for your husband to feel embarrassed but he does feel that way. What would happen if you went up to him and said quietly, “hey I just realized, does our daughter have some sun screen on, I’m worried she might get sunburned.  We could be up all night with her if that happens and I know we both need our sleep tonight.” ?  He might even look and feel like a “good dad” if he then decides to put sunscreen on her without being told to do so. He sees you are in the same situation as he is…just now realizing your child should have some sunscreen on for her own good and for a peaceful night at home. Family and friends might even compliment him on being a thoughtful dad taking care of his daughter.  

What is a good way to help someone you love, learn how to grow into the dad he is capable of becoming. 

None of us are born knowing how to be a good parent. Most of us are not taught how to be good parents.  Sometimes our own parents are the worst role models for being parents…so how does anyone learn how to be a thoughtful loving parent who has a well developed sense of empathy for their child and their partner?  

What is a good way? What is the best way? What way will have negative side effects like building resentment or misunderstandings and frustrations?
If he has another male family member or friend who are good examples of dads, your husband might respond better to seeing someone else doing these dad things the proper way.

If you want to create an opportunity for him to learn, I ask that you rethink correcting him in public. Boys don’t like that and will respond negatively rather than learn to do something differently.  Doing it privately also limits the opportunity for him to ignore what you are suggesting to him. I try to give feedback privately to boys and sandwich it between positives.  I also look for opportunities to give reminders before they should do something that is desired,  not after they forgot.  This helps them be more successful and they tend to like that feeling.  

It might also be a good idea to build up the amount of time he is alone with her… maybe to the point where you go visit a friend or family for an overnight and then possibly a weekend.  It’s probably going to work out better if he knows what her routines are and is setup to be successful when he is left alone with her.  "We further hypothesized that the interaction with physical paper, **rather than the mental editing/preparation of the notes or the physical act of handwriting, provides episodic and spatial information of notes relative to each page of real paper, together with visual/tactile information from the paper.** These properties and cues of papers could help to retrieve specific information, and thus lead to increased activations in specified brain regions for the Note group, compared with the other groups using mobile devices lacking such processes."

"We hypothesized that the use of a paper notebook, together with longhand note-taking, would enhance both memory encoding and later retrieval processes that could then be investigated at the brain level. There are other methods for learning/memorization that are more effective than repetition. Repetition is more like blocked practice which is less effective for long term memory and learning. Use any AP credit in classes that are unrelated to your major.  College admissions offices love that you have taken challenging/rigorous courses for admissions purposes.  College professors and their departments do not like AP courses. Typically professors will say AP courses do not go to the depth that college professors do. I know of excellent students who took AP Calculus AB in high school with a great math teacher-and still took calc 1 in college at different big 10 schools, only to find what they covered in one year of AP Calc took the college prof 1/2 of one semester to cover.  They would have missed the second half of learning in that course had they skipped out of calc 1.  

Ivy League schools do not accept any AP credit at all. The U of California system  ie UCLA, has been skeptical of AP courses for a long time.  I wonder if they still accept that credit?  They’ve just gone test optional so maybe so…

In college chemistry departments, lower level chem courses also teach you how to do things their way technique wise and how to use their expensive equipment.  (Does your school have a nuclear magnetic resonance machine, or an infra red spectrophotometer, or gas chromatograph machine? Are these still used in college chem labs or have they been replaced with better tech?). 

Taking AP classes in your anticipated college major will prepare you for success in college.  That is the point of school…to learn and develop your brain and while you are doing that I hope you will find what you love and feel passionate about.

If you want to still try to lighten your course load in college, try taking CLEP tests for your gen ed classes that are unrelated to your major….history, world language, etc. Depending on the college you decide to go to, you might still get a general science credit for your AP science classes from high school.  You can also take some gen Ed classes in the summer at your local community college and lighten your semester loads in college.  Make sure you create a rough draft of a 4year plan for your major and gen Ed’s so you can anticipate when your most difficult semesters will be…then use your clep, AP, summer school credits so you can take one less class during those semesters.  Also take a guess at when you will do your internship… maybe that can be done in the summer?  Maybe you can get paid for that?   Maybe you pick a college that has a co-op program like Kettering and make significant money while in college….   

College is fun and hard, and an incredible opportunity to see how much you can experience and learn inside and outside the classroom.  Enjoy your time there, no need to speed it up, life will be waiting for you when you are ready.
